newsitem.title: UK: Study finds ideal weight for British men.
newsitem.headline: Study finds ideal weight for British men.

text.p: British doctors said they had found the ideal weight for a man who wants to have the best health possible, and it is slightly leaner than average.
They said a body mass index -- a commonly used measurement based on a ration of height to weight -- of 22 seemed to be the most desirable.
Body mass index (BMI) is reckoned by dividing the weight in kilograms by height in centimetres squared.

For example, a man 170 cm (five feet seven inches) tall weighing 70 kg (154 pounds) would have a BMI of 24, which is in the healthy zone. To have the recommended BMI of 22 he would have to get his weight down to 65 kg.

Gerald Shaper of London's Royal Free Hospital and colleagues studied the records of nearly 8,000 men aged 40 to 59. They grouped them into five different BMI categories and analysed deaths and illnesses.
Most who died, 971 out of 1,271, did so from heart attacks. There were 290 strokes and 245 new cases of diabetes, which is linked with weight.

"Risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack and diabetes increased progressively from an index of 20 even after age, smoking, social class, alcohol consumption and physical activity were adjusted for," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
The overall lowest risk of death was in men in the 20 to 23.9 range.

"These findings strongly suggest that the healthy, biologically normal or optimum body weight in these middle-aged men is towards the lower end of the range which is currently regarded as acceptable," Shaper's group concluded.

BMI has been widely used by doctors and insurance companies for more than 20 years. Experts say it takes into account differences in build, although extremely heavily muscled athletes may be an exception.
It works for both men and women.
Someone with a BMI of less than 19 is considered underweight, 19 to 25 is healthy, 26 to 30 is overweight and above 30 obese. A BMI of 41 is considered very obese.
